Adulteress
ă-dŭl´tẽr-ĕs
n. (a married woman unfaithful to her husband — Hebrew naaph; Greek moichalis)
Latin adultera, from adulterare, to corrupt or falsify. The word names the falsifying of a covenant, not merely an act.

Biblical Definition

Adulteress names a woman who has broken the marriage covenant, and Scripture uses the word with equal weight upon the man. The law is explicit: “the man that committeth adultery with another man's wife, even he that committeth adultery with his neighbour's wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death” (Lev 20:10) — both, in one sentence, with no double standard. Proverbs warns the young man of what it costs: “by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life” (Pro 6:26). Paul uses the term in a legal argument about the believer's release from the law: “if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law” (Rom 7:3). And Hosea receives the hardest command given to any prophet: “Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine” (Hos 3:1). The comparison is stated by God Himself. Israel is the adulteress; the LORD is the husband who goes and buys her back. Every doctrine of covenant love in Scripture has to reckon with that chapter.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an adulteress as a married woman guilty of incontinence; and, in Scripture, an idolatress, or a soul unfaithful to God.

expand to see more

ADUL'TERESS, n. A married woman guilty of incontinence.

ADUL'TERER, n. A man guilty of adultery; a man who has sexual commerce with any married woman, except his wife.

2. In Scripture, an idolater.

ADUL'TERY, n. Violation of the marriage bed; a crime, or a civil injury, which introduces confusion of progeny.

Key Scripture

Romans 7:3 — "So then if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law; so that she is no adulteress, though she be married to another man."

Hosea 3:1 — "Then said the LORD unto me, Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine."

Leviticus 20:10 — "And the man that committeth adultery with another man's wife, even he that committeth adultery with his neighbour's wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death."

Proverbs 6:26 — "For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life."

Modern Corruption

Adultery is reclassified as a private matter between consenting adults, and the covenant it breaks — along with the God who witnesses it — is left out of the accounting.

expand to see more

The modern reckoning treats adultery as a failure of a relationship rather than the breaking of a covenant, and therefore as a matter for the parties alone. Malachi answers directly: the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, and He hates putting away. A marriage in Scripture has three parties, and the third does not leave when the vows grow inconvenient. This is also why Proverbs speaks of the adulteress hunting for the precious life — the injury reaches past reputation and property into the soul, and both the man and the woman in the case are said to destroy their own.

Two guards must be set on this word. First, Scripture's standard is even-handed: Leviticus condemns the adulterer and the adulteress in one clause, and the Lord dealt far more sharply with the men who dragged a woman before Him than with her. A church that whispers about women and excuses men has not learned the law it claims to keep. Second, Hosea 3 forbids the conclusion that such a sinner is beyond love. God commanded a prophet to go and love an adulteress, buy her back at the price of a slave, and keep her — and said plainly that this was according to the love of the LORD toward Israel. The condemnation and the redemption are in the same Bible and often in the same chapter.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naaph (H5003), to commit adultery, literally and of idolatry — Leviticus 20:10, Hosea 3:1; Greek moichalis (G3428), an adulteress — Romans 7:3, Matthew 12:39 of an adulterous generation.

expand to see more

Hebrew naaph (H5003) — to commit adultery; Leviticus 20:10, Exodus 20:14, Jeremiah 3:8 of Israel's spiritual adultery.

Greek moichalis (G3428) — an adulteress; Romans 7:3, James 4:4, Matthew 12:39 and 16:4 of an adulterous generation.

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to go a whoring; the companion word in the prophets for covenant unfaithfulness.

Hosea 3:2 records the price Hosea paid to buy her back: fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley.

Romans 7 uses the marriage law as an argument: death dissolves the bond, and the believer is dead to the law by the body of Christ.

Usage

"“The adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death” — both, in one clause."

"“The adulteress will hunt for the precious life”."

"“Go yet, love a woman… yet an adulteress” — and God says why."
